You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from excessive computational overhead due to the processing of dense modality tokens. While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer a trade-off between capacity and efficiency, current approaches typically require building new sparse structures and training from scratch, which is resource-intensive. There is a lack of methodology to leverage the redundancy within *existing, well-trained* dense MLLMs. A significant barrier to converting these dense models into dynamic ones is the "feature gap": naively skipping layers in a pre-trained model drastically alters the feature space, leading to performance collapse. Furthermore, standard training objectives do not incentivize the model to seek computational shortcuts, making it difficult to learn efficient routing pathways.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that a standard, well-trained MLLM already possesses the characteristics of a Mixture-of-Experts system, where specific layers are only necessary for specific types of inputs. We propose that we can transform a frozen dense MLLM into a dynamic routing network by treating entire layers as "experts." By introducing a mechanism to dynamically bypass heavy layers in favor of lightweight connections, we believe we can achieve example-dependent optimal path routing. Our core intuition is that by bridging the feature gap with low-rank adapters and enforcing structural sparsity, we can unlock significant inference acceleration without needing to retrain the backbone model.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a framework termed "Routing Experts" (RoE) to convert dense models into sparse ones. Our strategy involves the following conceptual components:

*   **Layer-as-Expert Architecture:** We will conceptualize each layer of the pre-trained MLLM as an independent expert block. The inference process will become a dynamic path selection where the model decides which blocks are required for the current input.
*   **Adapter-Based Skip Connections:** To address the feature gap caused by skipping layers, we will not simply use identity mappings for skipped layers. Instead, we will implement lightweight adapters as alternative, low-cost pathways. When a heavy layer is bypassed, the signal will flow through the adapter to perform necessary but efficient feature transformation, ensuring the feature space remains consistent for subsequent layers.
*   **Context-Aware Routing Tokens:** To handle the misalignment between training (often multi-turn conversations) and dynamic inference, we will insert learnable "routing tokens" into the input sequence. These tokens will aggregate information from the image and text queries to generate layer-wise routing decisions, allowing the model to switch paths dynamically for different turns in a conversation.
*   **Difficulty-Aware Sparsity Regularization:** We will introduce a training objective that actively encourages layer skipping. To ensure the model retains capacity for hard tasks, this regularization will be weighted by the difficulty of the example (inferred from the loss). This forces the model to learn short-cut pathways for easy examples while utilizing the full depth of the network for complex reasoning.

## Expected Contribution
We expect to establish a new paradigm for efficient MLLM deployment that bypasses the need for expensive pre-training of MoE architectures. Theoretically, this will demonstrate that "densely" trained models contain high degrees of extractable sparsity. Practically, this approach aims to provide a plug-and-play solution that significantly accelerates the inference speed of existing state-of-the-art models while maintaining competitive performance across diverse vision-language tasks.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We implemented a method to transform existing Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into dynamic mixture-of-experts systems by routing (skipping) layers during inference.

*   **Datasets:** We utilized five common vision-language benchmarks and five MLLM-specific benchmarks.
    *   **Common VL Benchmarks:** VQAv2, GQA, ScienceQA (SQA), VizWiz, and TextVQA. We used data splits organized in the LLaVA-1.5 instruction format.
    *   **MLLM-Specific Benchmarks:** POPE, MME, MMB (MMBench), SEED (SEED-Bench), and MM-Vet.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Accuracy:** Reported for VQAv2, GQA, SQA, VizWiz, TextVQA, POPE, MMB, SEED.
    *   **Score:** Reported for MME and MM-Vet.
    *   **Inference Speed:** Measured in samples per second (and tokens per second for qualitative analysis).
    *   **Skip Rate:** The percentage of layers skipped during inference (actual skip rate).
    *   **L1-Distance:** Used in preliminary analysis to measure feature impact per layer.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Dense MLLMs:** Qwen-VL (9.6B), Qwen-VL-Chat (9.6B), LLaVA-1.5 (Vicuna-7B), VILA (Vicuna-7B), LLaVA-HR (Vicuna-7B).
    *   **Sparse MLLMs:** MoE-LLaVA-1.6B×4 (StableLM-1.6B base), MoE-LLaVA-2.7B×4 (Phi-2.7B base).
    *   **Ablation Baselines:** LLaVA equipped with Routers only, LLaVA with Routers + Sparsity Regularization (but no adapters).
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Base Models:** LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-HR, and VILA.
    *   **Adapter Configuration:** The hidden dimension of the adapter-based skip connections was set to 1,024.
    *   **Regularization:** The hyper-parameter $\alpha$ for controlling sparsity regularization impact was set to 0.5.
    *   **Training Data:** We sampled subsets of the 665k LLaVA-1.5 instruction data for the three-stage training process: 15% for RoE-LLaVA, 10% for RoE-LLaVA-HR, and 25% for RoE-VILA.
    *   **Optimization:**
        *   MLLM Learning Rate: $2 \times 10^{-6}$.
        *   Router/Adapter Learning Rate: $4 \times 10^{-4}$.
        *   Epochs: 1.
        *   Strategy: Early stopping applied.
    *   **Hardware:** Training time was measured in GPU hours using NVIDIA A800 GPUs.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Layer-wise Contribution Analysis:**
*   We calculated the L1-distances between input and output features of each layer in LLaVA-7B. We observed that some layers had low L1-distances, indicating they contributed less to the feature update.
*   We observed that the layer contribution profiles differed between examples (e.g., distinguishing between "farmer" vs "dog" images).

**Skip Rate and Task Complexity:**
*   We found that the actual skip rate of RoE was dependent on the task difficulty.
*   The model exhibited higher skip rates on multiple-choice questions (e.g., 23.03% on SQA) compared to open-ended questions (e.g., 8.81% on GQA).
*   Visual analysis showed that for simple questions (e.g., "Is there any fried chicken?"), the model skipped more layers (shown as yellow bars in visualizations) compared to detailed questions about the same image.
*   Visual analysis also showed that for the same question type ("How many people?"), the model skipped more layers on simpler visual scenes compared to complex classroom scenes.

**Comparison with Baselines:**
*   We observed that RoE-LLaVA generated answers that were as detailed and accurate as the dense LLaVA baseline, whereas the sparse MoE-LLaVA baseline produced briefer responses.
*   In token generation speed analysis (tokens/s), RoE-LLaVA outperformed both LLaVA and MoE-LLaVA. For specific examples, speedups were observed up to 13.9% over LLaVA and 77.3% over MoE-LLaVA.

**Ablation Findings:**
*   Directly adding routers without regularization resulted in a negligible skip rate (average 1.1%), indicating the model preferred the default pathway.
*   Adding routers decreased inference speed (+7.29% latency) due to overhead without achieving sparsity.
*   Using sparsity regularization without adapters increased the skip rate (to 14.72%) but caused significant performance degradation (e.g., -2.0% on SEED).
*   The addition of adapter-based skip connections recovered the performance loss caused by skipping.

**Sensitivity of Base Models:**
*   LLaVA-HR was observed to be more sensitive to layer skipping than LLaVA. An increase in skip rate from 7.68% to 12.02% in LLaVA-HR resulted in a ~4.34% average performance drop.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The integration of visual tokens into Large Language Models (LLMs) to create Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly exacerbated computational overhead. While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer a trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency, current approaches typically involve constructing new sparse structures with multiple parallel Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) and training them from scratch. This ignores the potential of existing, well-trained dense MLLMs.

However, converting a pre-trained dense MLLM into a dynamic, sparse model presents three significant challenges:
1.  **Feature Space Discontinuity:** Simply skipping layers in a well-trained model causes drastic shifts in the feature space, leading to performance collapse.
2.  **Inertia of Dense Pathways:** End-to-end trained models are optimized for fixed pathways and resist layer skipping during post-training.
3.  **Granularity Mismatch:** Existing MLLM training often packs multiple multi-turn conversations into a single example. A global routing decision is insufficient; we require fine-grained, example-dependent routing that aligns training with inference.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that a standard, well-trained MLLM can be transformed into a dynamic Mixture-of-Experts model without structural overhaul. We hypothesize that by treating each existing layer as an "expert" and introducing a lightweight **adapter-based skip connection** as an alternative path, we can dynamically route tokens to skip redundant computation. By employing a specialized **Routing Token** mechanism and a **Structure Sparsity Regularization**, we can teach the model to select the optimal, shortest inference path for each example, thereby reducing computation while preserving the feature transformation capabilities of the original model.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework termed **Routing Experts (RoE)**. This framework transforms a static $n$-layer MLLM into a dynamic network where each layer serves as a candidate expert that can be bypassed in favor of a computationally inexpensive adapter.

### 1. Dynamic Expert Construction and Routing
In a standard MLLM, the inference path is a fixed sequence of layers $G = G_1 \circ G_2 \circ \dots \circ G_n$. We will redefine the network as a dynamic composition of modules $M_i$, where the router determines whether to utilize the original heavy layer $G_i$ or a lightweight adapter $A_i$.

The dynamic expert pathway $G'$ will be defined as:
$$ G' = M_1 \circ M_2 \circ \dots \circ M_n $$
The selection logic for the $i$-th module $M_i$ is governed by a routing function $R_i$:
$$ M_i = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} G_i, & \text{if } R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)_0 > R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)_1 \\ A_i, & \text{if } R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)_0 \leq R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)_1 \end{array} \right. $$
Here, $R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)$ is a binary probability distribution indicating the choice between the original layer (index 0) and the adapter (index 1).

**The Adapter Mechanism:**
To bridge the feature gap caused by skipping a layer, we will implement $A_i$ as a low-rank adapter network. Given input $\mathbf{x}$, the adapter output $\mathbf{x}'$ is calculated as:
$$ \mathbf{x}' = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_d)\mathbf{W}_u $$
where $\mathbf{W}_d \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times c}$ and $\mathbf{W}_u \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times d}$ are learnable weight matrices with bottleneck dimension $c \ll d$. This ensures that skipping the heavy layer $G_i$ still allows for necessary feature space transformation with minimal computational cost.

### 2. Routing Token Formulation
To enable fine-grained control over routing within multi-turn conversations and align training with inference, we will introduce learnable **Routing Tokens** ($\mathbf{r}$). We will inject these tokens into the input sequence before the image and before each question.

The augmented input sequence $\mathbf{x}_i$ will be structured as:
$$ \mathbf{x}_i = [\mathbf{r}_i^{(0)}, \mathbf{I}_i, \mathbf{r}_i^{(1)}, \mathbf{Q}_i^{(1)}, \mathbf{A}_i^{(1)}, \dots, \mathbf{r}_i^{(q)}, \mathbf{Q}_i^{(q)}, \mathbf{A}_i^{(q)}] $$
where:
*   $\mathbf{I}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_v \times d}$ are visual tokens.
*   $\mathbf{Q}_i^{(k)}$ and $\mathbf{A}_i^{(k)}$ represent the question and answer tokens for the $k$-th turn.
*   $\mathbf{r}_i^{(0)}$ is the router token for the image, and $\mathbf{r}_i^{(k)}$ ($k > 0$) is the router token for the $k$-th question.

The routing weights for the $j$-th question-answer pair will be computed based on the aggregated information in the routing tokens:
$$ R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)^{(j)} = \mathrm{Softmax}\left(\frac{1}{\tau} [\mathbf{r}_i^{(0)}, \mathbf{r}_i^{(j)}] \mathbf{W}_r\right), \quad j > 0 $$
where $[\cdot, \cdot]$ denotes concatenation, $\mathbf{W}_r \in \mathbb{R}^{2d \times 2}$ is the routing weight matrix, and $\tau$ is a temperature parameter.

### 3. Optimization and Sparsity Regularization
To overcome the model's tendency to utilize the full network, we will design a **Structure Sparsity Regularization** term $\mathcal{L}_s$. This objective forces the average skip rate to meet a predefined target $t$:
$$ \mathcal{L}_s = \max\left(t - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)_1, 0\right) $$
where $n$ is the total number of layers, and $R_i(\mathbf{x}_i)_1$ represents the probability of choosing the adapter (skipping the layer).

We will combine this with the standard tuning loss $\mathcal{L}_t$. To ensure that easier examples are routed through sparser paths while difficult examples retain capacity, we will weight the regularization by the difficulty of the example (approximated by its loss value):
$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_t + \alpha e^{-|\mathcal{L}_t|} \mathcal{L}_s $$
where $\alpha$ is a hyper-parameter balancing performance and sparsity. This formulation ensures that when the prediction error $|\mathcal{L}_t|$ is low (easy example), the weight of the sparsity penalty increases, encouraging the router to skip layers.

### 4. Training Scheme
We will implement a three-stage training strategy to ensure stability:
1.  **Adapter Warmup:** Freeze the MLLM backbone. Randomly select pathways to train only the adapter connections $A_i$ to ensure they are capable of feature transformation.
2.  **Router Warmup:** Freeze the MLLM backbone. Train both adapters and routers using the sparsity regularization $\mathcal{L}_s$ to initialize optimal pathfinding.
3.  **Instruction Tuning:** Unfreeze the full model (or apply LoRA) and train jointly with $\mathcal{L}$ to align the backbone, adapters, and routers.

## Expected Contribution
This research expects to deliver three primary contributions to the field of Multi-modal LLMs:
1.  **Theoretical Feasibility of Retrofitted MoE:** We will demonstrate that dense, pre-trained MLLMs contain inherent sparse subnetworks ("dynamic experts") that can be activated without architecture re-design.
2.  **Efficient Inference:** By effectively routing tokens through lightweight adapters for "easy" samples or layers, we expect to significantly increase inference speed (samples per second) compared to dense baselines.
3.  **Training Efficiency:** Unlike standard MoE models that require training from scratch, our approach leverages existing checkpoints, requiring only a fraction of the data and compute for the adaptation process.

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-sonnet-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
